title: Rewrite `(a, b) -> a.compareTo(b)` as `String::compareTo`.
keyPoints: A two-argument lambda calling an instance method on its first argument can be an unbound method reference
The first parameter becomes the receiver; the second becomes the method's argument
This matches Comparator<String> because compare(a, b) maps to a.compareTo(b)
For natural ordering, Comparator.naturalOrder() is even clearer than String::compareTo
The bound form someString::compareTo fixes the receiver and takes only one argument

s1_definition.oneliner: (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b) equals String::compareTo: the first argument is the receiver, the second is the method's argument.
s1_definition.profdef:
- An **unbound two-argument reference** `Type::instanceMethod` maps the first parameter to the receiver and the second to the method argument.
- `String::compareTo` satisfies `Comparator<String>` because `compare(a, b)` calls `a.compareTo(b)`.
- The **bound form** `someString::compareTo` fixes the receiver and leaves only the argument.
- For **natural ordering**, `Comparator.naturalOrder()` is clearer and supports null layering.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya at the National Bank of India compares two account names alphabetically. Instead of saying 'take name A and ask it to compare itself with name B', she just points at the compareTo skill and lets Java supply the two names in order.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Lambda: (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b)
    first param 'a' → receiver of compareTo
    second param 'b' → argument of compareTo

  Method reference: String::compareTo
    Compiler maps:
      compare(a, b) → a.compareTo(b)

  Both satisfy: Comparator<String>
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When a two-argument lambda calls an instance method on its first argument and passes the second as the method's argument, rewrite it as an unbound method reference. (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b) becomes String::compareTo, where the compiler maps the first parameter to the receiver and the second to compareTo's argument.

At the National Bank of India, this sorts account holder names alphabetically with names.sort(String::compareTo). For natural ordering, Comparator.naturalOrder() is even clearer and supports null layering with nullsFirst.

The key distinction is unbound vs bound: String::compareTo takes two parameters (the receiver and the argument), while "Rajesh"::compareTo fixes the receiver and takes only the argument.

Remember one sentence: String::compareTo replaces (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b), with the first parameter as the receiver and the second as the argument.
